analysis.one_liner: Makes the president's anticompetitive-regulation executive order permanent federal law.
analysis.headline: Introduced August 1, 2025, the bill has no cosponsors and has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee with no action since that day.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write President Trump's April 2025 executive order on reducing anticompetitive regulatory barriers directly into federal law, so a future president could not simply revoke it. The order directs federal agencies to find and remove rules that shield incumbent businesses from competition — including state occupational licensing and hospital "certificate of need" requirements — and puts the Federal Trade Commission to work on them. The bill itself is a single sentence long, has no cosponsors, and has not moved since its referral to the House Judiciary Committee in August 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers shut out of licensed trades by expensive licensing requirements, patients in markets where certificate-of-need rules let incumbent hospitals block rivals, and new small businesses trying to enter regulated industries. Consumers generally gain when rules that protect incumbents from competition are loosened and prices fall.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers blocked by licensing rules and consumers

how_it_helps.text: Would give the force of law to the executive order's directives that federal agencies identify and remove regulations that block competition, instead of leaving them to an order any future president could revoke

The executive order it codifies targets state occupational licensing and hospital certificate-of-need rules — requirements that workers pay hundreds of dollars and years of training to enter a trade, and that hospitals must clear to expand or open — which tend to raise prices and keep people out of work

Putting the order into statute would also direct the Federal Trade Commission to keep using its authority against anticompetitive state and federal barriers rather than leaving that effort to executive discretion

analysis.who_pays: Licensed professionals whose boards limit entry and protect their earnings; hospitals and other incumbent providers whose market position rests on certificate-of-need approval; and state governments, which would face sustained federal pressure to unwind the licensing systems they control.
analysis.who_pays_short: Licensed incumbents and state licensing systems

drawbacks.text: The bill copies the entire executive order into law in a single sentence, without defining which regulations count as 'anticompetitive barriers'; the same review process could be aimed at rules that protect health, safety, or wages, stripping away protections under a competition label
It would put sustained federal pressure on state licensing decisions, a federal intrusion into systems states have traditionally controlled
With zero cosponsors and no committee action, the bill has never received any scrutiny — no hearings, no testimony on which specific rules would actually be affected

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's underlying goal — fewer government-created advantages for incumbent businesses — would mainly help workers and consumers, and it is hard to defend occupational licensing rents or certificate-of-need protection as serving the public. But the drafting is blunt: one sentence turns the whole executive order into statute without saying which rules are in play, and a deregulatory review with a competition label can reach rules that also protect people. In practice, with no cosponsors and no movement in committee, its current value is symbolic.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and has sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams of Texas introduced the bill on August 1, 2025
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the record
The bill's entire operative text is a single sentence stating that Executive Order 14267 'shall have the force and effect of law'
No member of the House from either party has signed on as a cosponsor

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet, so no one has concretely won or lost; for now, licensed professions and incumbent providers keep their existing protections while the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent licensed professions keep the status quo

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 1, 2025; the only member supporting it

for.name: President Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Issued Executive Order 14267 in April 2025; the bill would codify his order, though the administration has not acted on the bill itself

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jim Jordan)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearings or markup scheduled

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been held; the bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split has formed.

industries.industry: Licensed occupations (occupational licensing boards and licensees)
industries.note: Licensing boards limit who can work in a trade and protect incumbents' earnings by restricting entry. The executive order the bill codifies puts federal pressure on states to loosen these barriers, which would expose licensees to competition while opening the trades to more workers.

industries.industry: Hospitals and health systems protected by certificate-of-need laws
industries.note: Certificate-of-need rules let incumbent hospitals block new competitors and expansions, which tends to raise costs for patients. The codified order targets such anticompetitive barriers, threatening that protection.

industries.industry: Small businesses and new entrants in regulated trades
industries.note: New firms and workers face the licensing and approval barriers that incumbents use to keep competitors out; codifying the competition directives would work in their favor.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action months after introduction, the bill is all but certain to die in committee when this Congress ends, as most referred bills do. It could be revived if the committee decided to hold a hearing, but nothing in the record suggests that is coming.
